title: Article 6 cooperative mechanisms
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

definition.text: The part of the 2015 Paris Agreement that sets out how countries may cooperate voluntarily to carry out their nationally determined contributions.

facts.text: It aims to allow higher ambition in mitigation and adaptation while promoting sustainable development, on condition of environmental integrity, transparency and robust accounting.
It has three pathways: cooperative approaches that trade ITMOs (6.2), a UN-supervised crediting mechanism (6.4) and non-market approaches (6.8).
The core 'Article 6 rulebook' was adopted at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, and later decisions have focused on putting it into practice.
It succeeds the Kyoto Protocol's flexible mechanisms, with the transition expected to be completed by 2025.
Its impact is debated, especially over environmental integrity, governance capacity and the risk of over-crediting.

contested_note: Analysts debate whether Article 6 transfers mainly lower costs and mobilise finance or undermine integrity through over-crediting, weak baselines and 'hot air'.

title: Internationally transferred mitigation outcomes
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Article 6.2: Cooperative approaches

definition.text: Measured emission reductions or removals that one country transfers to another under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement and that count toward the buyer's NDC.

facts.text: Article 6.2 lets countries trade them through bilateral or multilateral deals without using the central crediting mechanism.
They can be expressed in tonnes of CO2-equivalent or other metrics, and can come from crediting projects or from linked emissions trading systems.
By 2024 over 80 bilateral agreements were in place; the first completed trade, between Thailand and Switzerland, was reported in January 2024.

contested_note: Commentators disagree on whether these transfers mainly cut costs or risk over-crediting and 'hot air'.

title: Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (Article 6.4)

definition.text: A UN-supervised scheme set up under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement that registers emission-cutting activities and issues credits for verified reductions or removals.

facts.text: Its credits are called Article 6.4 emission reductions (A6.4ERs) and are tracked in a registry with unique identifiers.
A share of proceeds goes to the Adaptation Fund, and a portion of units is cancelled to deliver an overall mitigation in global emissions.
Activities are validated, registered, monitored and independently verified before units are issued, under the oversight of the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body.

title: Non-market approaches (Article 6.8)
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Article 6.8: Non-market approaches

definition.text: Voluntary cooperation between countries under Article 6.8 of the Paris Agreement that involves no international transfer of emission reductions.

facts.text: They can combine mitigation and adaptation and involve finance, technology transfer and capacity building.
A work programme and the Glasgow Committee on Non-market Approaches were set up at COP26 in 2021; the committee began work in 2022.

title: Corresponding adjustment
article: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement#Accounting, reporting and transparency architecture

definition.text: The accounting step that makes sure an emission reduction transferred between countries is counted in only one country's NDC.

facts.text: It guards against double counting, which covers double issuance, double claiming by two countries and double use of one unit.
Countries must report what they authorise, transfer, acquire, cancel or use, and how this shows up in their NDC accounting.
Registries recording issuance, transfer, cancellation and use make the tracking possible.

definition.text: A country's own pledge, under the Paris Agreement, of how it will cut greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change.

facts.text: NDCs are described as being at the heart of the Paris Agreement; each country decides for itself what to contribute.
They must be renewed every five years, and each should be more ambitious than the last, a rule called the principle of progression.
The pledges themselves are not binding, but preparing, communicating and updating them is; there is no way to force a country to meet its target.
Some pledges are unconditional, while others depend on outside finance, technical support or other countries' ambition.
They are the first UNFCCC emission targets that apply equally to developed and developing countries.
Emission cuts must rise 80% beyond current NDCs to likely meet 2 °C; on current trends the chance of staying below 2 °C is only 5%.

definition.text: The initial, voluntary and non-binding climate pledges countries made before the 2015 Paris Agreement, which became their first NDCs.

facts.text: UNFCCC parties were asked to publish them at the 2013 Warsaw climate conference.
The term was a compromise between Kyoto's binding 'QELROs' for developed countries and 'NAMAs' for developing ones.
Switzerland submitted the first on 27 February 2015; 85% of surveyed countries said the short time frame was a challenge.

title: Ratchet mechanism

definition.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly cycle of reporting, review and new pledges, designed to raise countries' climate ambition over time.

facts.text: Countries publish biennial progress reports that undergo technical review.
These feed a global stocktake, on an offset five-year cycle, that judges whether all NDCs together are enough.
The stocktake's findings are meant to shape each country's next, more ambitious pledge.

notes: Title 'Ratchet mechanism' is a common name; the cited section speaks of a framework 'designed to ratchet up climate action over time'.
